''Senecio glastifolius'' is a flowering plant found throughout the world and native to [[South Africa]]. It has a collection of common names throughout the world. The two common names in [[New Zealand]] are '''pink ragwort''' and '''holly-leaved senecio'''.<ref name=":0">{{Cite web |title=Senecio glastifolius |url=https://www.nzpcn.org.nz/flora/species/senecio-glastifolius/ |access-date=2025-05-11 |website=New Zealand Plant Conservation Network |language=en}}</ref> In the [[United Kingdom|UK]] the most common names are '''woad leaved ragwort''', '''holly leaved groundsel''', and '''lilac senecio'''.<ref name=":1">{{Cite thesis |last=Beautrais |first=Josef Rehua |title=The geographic distribution of Senecio glastifolius in New Zealand: past, current and climatic potential |date=2013-01-01 |degree=thesis |publisher=Open Access Te Herenga Waka-Victoria University of Wellington |url=https://openaccess.wgtn.ac.nz/articles/thesis/The_geographic_distribution_of_Senecio_glastifolius_in_New_Zealand_past_current_and_climatic_potential/17005594/1 |doi=10.26686/wgtn.17005594.v1 |language=en}}</ref><ref name=":2">{{Cite journal |last=Rapson |first=Gillian L |date=2017-11-10 |title=Senecio glastifolius (holly-leaved senecio) |journal=CABI Compendium |volume=CABI Compendium |article-number=117070 |doi=10.1079/cabicompendium.117070|doi-access=free }}</ref> In [[South Africa]] it is called '''senecio''', '''waterdissel''', and '''water thistle'''.<ref name=":1" /> In the [[United States|USA]] it is referred to as '''lilac–flowered groundsel.'''<ref name=":2" /> Finally, there is the less common name of '''purple ragwort'''.<ref name=":1" /> 

==Description==
''Senecio glastifolius'' is an upright perennial [[Herbaceous plant|herbaceous]] plant in the family [[Asteraceae]].<ref name=":2" /> In New Zealand it commonly grows to around 1 meter tall although some individuals in sheltered areas can grow upwards of two meters.<ref name=":1" /><ref name=":2" /> The stems of the plant are glabrous (smooth and hairless) and often woody in the lower areas of the plant.<ref name=":2" /> The main stem can be 8-12 cm in diameter at the base of larger plants before branching to smaller stems.<ref name=":3">{{Cite journal |last1=Williams |first1=P.A. |last2=Ogle |first2=C.C. |last3=Timmins |first3=S.M. |last4=La Cock |first4=G. |last5=Reid |first5=V. |date=1999 |title=Biology and ecology of Senecio glastifolius and its spread and impacts in New Zealand / P.A. Williams |url=https://www.doc.govt.nz/globalassets/documents/science-and-technical/sfc112.pdf |journal=Science for Conservation |volume=12 |via=Department of Conservation}}</ref> The stems branch from near the base and are green in colour with red ridges running vertically along the length of the stem.<ref name=":2" />  

The leaves are arranged alternately along the stems and appear like the leaf of a holly.<ref name=":2" /> They are elliptic (oval-shaped) and bright to deep green in colour with large irregular teeth along the margin of the leaf which gives them a prickly texture.<ref name=":2" /> The base of leaves are apetiolate (stalkless) at the base and clasping, wrapping partly around the stem especially in young plants.<ref name=":2" /> Leaves range from 3-15cm long and 2-3cm wide; leaves lower on the plant are often larger and more serrated compared to upper leaves which are smaller and less toothed.<ref name=":2" /><ref name=":3" /> Leaves are located every 1-2 cm along the stem.<ref name=":2" /> 

The flowers are grouped into heads called capitula, similar to the flower of a daisy.<ref name=":2" />  The heads are arranged in loose, flat-topped clusters called [[Corymb|corymbs]], which contain 20 – 30 capitula each, with some plants producing several hundred giving a complete covering of flowers over the foliage.<ref name=":2" />  Each [[Pseudanthium|capitulum]] is about 40-50mm in diameter and surrounded by a ring of 19-23 [[Bract|bracts]], which are small leaf-like structures that protect the flowers.<ref name=":2" /> Each bract is 6-9 mm long and tipped with a tiny dark point.<ref name=":3" /> 

Each capitulum contains two types of flowers: central disk [[florets]] which are yellow and 6-8mm long, and outer ray florets, which resemble petals and range from deep pink and purple, to mauve, or white.<ref name=":2" /> Most often they are bright pink and 12-25mm long arranged in a ring around the flower head.<ref name=":2" /><ref name=":3" /> 

The fruit of ''S. glastifolius'' is a dry, seed structure known as an [[achene]], which is 2-2.5mm long and dark brown.<ref name=":2" /> Achenes from the ray florets are glabrous and those from disc florets are hairy.<ref name=":2" /> Each seed is topped with a pappus – a tuft of fine hair-like structure that aids in wind dispersals; each pappus is 7-9mm long and falls off after dispersal.<ref name=":2" /><ref name=":3" />

''Senecio glastifolius'' is sometimes confused with ''[[Senecio elegans]]'' (which also grows by the coast), but the leaves of the two species are different.  

[[File:Senecio glastifolius, in NZ opposite Kapiti Island.JPG|none|thumb|Leaves of ''Senecio glastifolius,'' showing the distinctively serrated margins. Photograph by Stephenhartley.]]

== Range ==

=== Natural global range ===
''Senecio glastifolius'' is native to South Africa's western and eastern [[Cape Provinces]] where it occupies a relatively small coastal range.<ref name=":3" /> In addition to its native range, it  has been introduced throughout many regions including [[Australia]], [[British Isles]], [[New Zealand]], [[Madeira|Maderia]], [[France]] and the [[United States|USA]].<ref name=":2" /> In Australia, ''S.glastifolius'' is a listed weed on the National Environmental Alert list. In New Zealand it is banned for sale and propagation and is managed as a pest.<ref name=":1" /> 

=== New Zealand range ===
In New Zealand ''S.glastifolius'' was first recorded as naturalised in 1963 near [[Gisborne, New Zealand|Gisborne]].<ref name=":1" /> Initially it was of limited concern, but the population expanded significantly in the following 30 years.<ref name=":3" /> Today in New Zealand it can be found widely across coastal and lowland areas of the North Island, mainly in the [[Manawatū–Whanganui|Manawatu]] and [[Whanganui (electorate)|Whanganui]] region. It is also found in areas of the South Island around [[Canterbury Region|Canterbury]] and [[Marlborough District|Marlborough]].<ref name=":1" /><ref name=":2" />

==Habitat==
It favours a [[Mediterranean climate]], often coastal, and typically colonises disturbed soil. ''Senecio glastifolius'' thrives in areas of disturbance and is commonly found in a range of habitats, including coastal dunes, roadside embankments, rocky outcrops, damp areas, shrublands and the open understory of forests.<ref name=":2" /> It can quickly establish after disturbances such as fires and clearing of land.<ref name=":2" /><ref name=":3" />  

==Ecology==

===Life cycle/Phenology===
''Senecio glastifolius'' is regarded as a short-lived perennial herb.<ref name=":0" />  Individual plants can live between 3-5 years although some larger plants in sheltered conditions have survived 10 years potentially meaning ''S.glastifolius'' can survive a decade.<ref name=":2" /> 

Seeds germinate typically within two weeks.<ref name=":2" /> Maximum germination occurs when the temperature is warmer than 25 degrees.<ref name=":3" /> Germination success tends to be between 53% and 80% and in New Zealand germination has been observed between February and August.<ref name=":3" /> Disturbance from fires followed by rain can increase germination of seedlings.<ref name=":2" /> Seeds remain in the soil banks for several years and can be released from dormancy by disturbance such as cultivation or fire.<ref name=":2" /> In Western Australia the plants have been observed to grow between March and August like New Zealand.<ref name=":2" /> 

Flowering usually occurs in spring but some plants in New Zealand have been observed to have a second flowering in summer.<ref name=":2" /><ref name=":3" /> The capitula of ''S. glastifolius'' can produce up to 250 seeds each which are thought to be wind dispersed.<ref name=":2" /> Plants after flowering two to three time can become top heavy and break at the stem. Branches can continue to grow after this and there is some evidence of stems lying horizontal and in contact with soil forming new roots.<ref name=":3" /> 

===Preferred conditions ===
''Senecio glastifolius'' prefers a warm temperate climate with an average high temperature of more than 10 degrees, and low temperature of above 0.<ref name=":2" /> It can tolerate climates that are wet all year and temperate climates with dry summers (Rapson, 2017). It is wind resistant and can grow in full sun to lightly shaded areas.<ref name=":3" /> It can be found in a range of altitudes from 18m to 1090m.<ref name=":2" /> It can grow in a variety of soil types but it prefers a light texture, neutral soil pH, free drainage but can still tolerate high soil moisture.<ref name=":2" /><ref name=":3" />  

===Predators, Parasites, and Diseases===
Grazing pressure on ''S. glastifolius'' is often low, as the plant becomes unpalatable to livestock once stems become woody and the leaves become prickly in texture.<ref name=":1" />  Young plants may be grazed by livestock, so often it establishes in areas with low stocking rate.<ref name=":1" /><ref name=":4">{{Cite journal |last1=Kriticos |first1=D.J. |last2=Beautrais |first2=J. |last3=Dodd |first3=M.B. |date=2018 |title=WRASP: A spatial weed risk assessment tool reveals critical variations in weed risks |url=https://www.cabidigitallibrary.org/doi/pdf/10.5555/20193428986 |journal=21st Australasian Weeds Conference}}</ref> Research in South Africa suggests the moth ''[[Diota rostrata]]'' feeds on the plant.<ref name=":2" /> In New Zealand the native magpie moth (''[[Nyctemera annulata]]'') larvae are known to feed on the leaves of the plant. The diurnal moth ''[[Aglossa caprealis|Aglossa cuprealis]]'' feeds on its flowers.<ref name=":3" />  Chrysanthemum stunt viroid is the only known disease to affect ''S. glastifolius.''<ref name=":2" /> 

== Economic and Social Benefit ==
In some areas around the world it is sold as an [[ornamental plant]] in garden centres, and valued for its beautiful pink flowers.<ref name=":3" /> 

== Invasive Status ==
It has been known to [[Escaped plant|escape cultivation]] and become [[Introduced species|naturalized]] in areas of appropriate climate. ''S. glastifolius'' is considered an invasive species in New Zealand and Australia due to its ability to thrive in a range of habitats and rapidly spread.<ref name=":2" /> Detecting it early and removing seedlings is the most successful method of control. Removal of established stands is best done by hand pulling and pesticide.<ref name=":2" /><ref name=":4" />
